lesson.title: The 1890 Yardstick: The National Origins Act of 1924
lesson.summary: The Immigration Act of 1924 made restriction permanent, pushed the quota baseline back to the 1890 census to favor northern and western Europe, and closed the door almost entirely on Asian immigration.
lesson.body:
The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 had been designed as a stopgap, and in 1924 Congress replaced it with a much stricter and more permanent law: the Immigration Act of 1924, commonly known as the National Origins Act or the Johnson-Reed Act after its chief sponsors, Representative Albert Johnson and Senator David Reed. President Calvin Coolidge signed it into law in May 1924.

The new law cut the quota to 2 percent of each nationality's population, but the more consequential change was moving the baseline census year from 1910 back to 1890. That single change had an enormous effect, because in 1890 far fewer Italians, Poles, Russian Jews, and other southern and eastern Europeans had yet arrived in the United States. Basing quotas on 1890 population figures meant quotas for those countries shrank to a small fraction of what they had been, while Britain, Germany, and Ireland received large quotas that often went unfilled. This was not an accident of statistics; supporters of the law openly intended it to preserve the ethnic makeup of the country as it had existed before the New Immigration Wave.

The law also included a total exclusion clause barring immigration from Asia entirely. This built on the earlier Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and went further, overriding the 1907 to 1908 Gentlemen's Agreement that had allowed a limited flow of Japanese immigrants. The exclusion of Japanese immigrants specifically caused real diplomatic friction with Japan, since it singled out a nation the United States otherwise treated as a rising world power.

By 1929, the law's full national origins formula had been phased in, basing quotas on the estimated ancestry of the entire American population rather than simply the foreign-born, which reinforced the same bias toward northern and western Europe. Immigration from the Western Hemisphere, including Mexico and Canada, was exempted from the quota system, though other legal and practical barriers still limited it. The National Origins Act sharply reduced overall immigration to the United States and remained the basic framework of American immigration law for four decades, until the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 replaced it.
